The state temple of the Khmer king Indravarman I, built in the late 9th century at the centre of his capital Hariharalaya, today the Roluos group near Siem Reap in Cambodia. Its inscription is dated 881/82. It is the earliest temple mountain of the Khmer Empire built in sandstone: a stepped pyramid standing for Mount Meru, the centre of the Hindu cosmos, with a lingam of Shiva in the shrine at the top. It tied the king's rule to the god.

The site is about 900 by 700 m, laid out east to west in three enclosures with two moats, which stand for the oceans around Meru. A causeway lined with seven-headed naga serpents, the first of their kind in Khmer building, crosses the moats. Between them stand the remains of 22 brick shrines, and eight brick towers stand around the pyramid in the inner enclosure. The pyramid itself, 65 by 67 m at the base, rises in five levels; stone elephants guard the corners of the lower terraces and lions flank the stairs. Its gates and stairs have often been compared with those of Borobudur in Java, and some scholars see it as a model.

Bakong set the form for later temple mountains such as Phnom Bakheng and Pre Rup. The tower on the summit is a 12th-century rebuilding in the style of Angkor Wat, and Buddhist shrines were added in the 12th and 13th centuries. The French conservator Maurice Glaize rebuilt the pyramid in the 1930s by taking it apart and resetting the stones. A modern Buddhist monastery stands by its east gate.
